newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Portuguese novelist, Chinese poet tipped for Nobel.
newsitem.headline: Portuguese novelist, Chinese poet tipped for Nobel.

text.p: A Portuguese novelist and an exiled Chinese poet are among hot tips to win the 1996 Nobel Literature Prize, the world's most coveted award for writers, which will be announced on Thursday.

Although in the past Swedish newspapers have sometimes made educated guesses, publishing a book review or biography of the winner before the announcement, literary experts say there have been few credible advance predictions of the 1996 winner.
Portugal's Jose Saramago and Chinese poet Bei Dao, who lives in exile in Paris, are both names being dropped in literary circles as possible winners of the $1.12 million prize.

The Swedish Academy, the 18-member committee of academicians who select the winner, may rule out a choice of another poet considering the selection of Irish poet Seamus Heaney last year, some Nobel watchers say.
"This is one of the questions we all have: they probably won't give the prize to an English speaker and probably not to a poet," said Lars Linder, cultural journalist at Swedish daily Dagens Nyheter.
"A couple of names that have been going around in recent years are the Belgium author Hugo Claus, Mexican author Carlos Fuentes and Peruvian author Mario Vargas Llosa," said Linder.

Swedish bookseller Akademibokhandeln staff have thrown up names such as Claus, Cees Nooteboom of The Netherlands, Albanian Ismael Kadare, Trinidad-born V.S. Naipaul, and Portugual's Antonio Lobo Antunes.
"I don't think it will be a poet because there have been so many poets," said Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet's Anders Paulrud, who named Portugal's Saramago and Belgium's Claus as strong contenders.
"The Portuguese language has never gotten the prize," Paulrud told Reuters. "If I should bet on it, I would bet on Saramago."

In keeping with tradition, the winner of the award, which will be worth 7.4 million crowns ($1.12 million) this year, will be revealed at the Swedish Academy's meeting place in the stock exchange in Stockholm's mediaeval Old Town.

This year there is speculation that internal feuding is shaking the august committee that awards the prize, following news that academy member Knut Ahnlund was boycotting the Swedish Academy's weekly Thursday meetings.
Ahnlund, who accused linguistics professor and academy secretary Sture Allen of being power-hungry, would be the fourth member to stop attending academy deliberations.
Committee members are elected to the academy for life.

Allen, however, quelled media speculation that the selection of this year's winner was endangered when he said last month that the debate was going ahead with gusto and that 14 members were more than enough to chose a winner.
Other Nobel prizes are due to be announced next week.
The Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute will reveal the winner of the prize for medicine at 11 a.m. local time (0900 GMT) in Stockholm on October 7.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences will announce the winners of the economics prize on October 8 at 11.30 a.m. (0930 GMT) and of the physics and chemistry prizes at 11.45 a.m. (0945 GMT) and two p.m. (1200 GMT) respectively at the earliest.
The Nobel Peace Prize will be announced in Oslo on October 11 at 11 a.m. (0900 GMT).
